How mortgages here compare with three other countries

By a staff reporter · Posted Fri 9 Oct 2026 at 5:00am

Most home loans in this country are variable, which means a change in the cash rate reaches household budgets within weeks. That is unusual. In the first comparison country almost every borrower fixes for thirty years, and in the second the most common loans are fixed for between five and seven years.

The difference matters when interest rates move. A household with a thirty year fixed loan does not notice a rise for decades, while a household on a variable rate notices at the next repayment. Economists say this makes monetary policy faster acting here than almost anywhere else, because the central bank's decisions pass straight through to spending.

It also changes who carries the risk. Where long fixed terms are normal, lenders and investors carry the risk that rates rise. Where variable loans are normal, borrowers carry it. Each system has costs: long fixed terms are more expensive at the start, and borrowers who want to move house before the term ends can face large break fees unless the loan can be transferred.

The third comparison country sits between the two, with a deposit system that takes the place of monthly rent and loans that are often interest only for the first years. Researchers who have compared the four systems say none is clearly better, and that each reflects decisions made by governments and banks many decades ago that would be hard to reverse now.

For a borrower choosing today, the practical lesson is narrower. The gap between the rates offered on fixed and variable loans was smaller this year than in most of the past decade, one researcher said, which means the choice is more about certainty than about price.
